source_summary.Definition: Unnecessary gender-specific, gender-exclusive, or gender-assumptive wording in teaching content.
source_summary.Scenarios / Indicators: Generic gendered pronouns; gender-marked occupational terms; gendered collective/address terms; gendered/exclusionary examples or names; binary gender assumptions.
source_summary.Potential Concern Examples: “Every programmer should submit his code.”; “Ask the chairman for approval.”; “Hey guys, please submit your assignments.”
source_summary.Non-Concern Examples: “Every programmer should submit their code.”; “John should submit his code.”; “The case study examines experiences reported by women in engineering.”
source_summary.Context Considerations: Do not flag gendered language simply because gender is mentioned. Consider whether gender is relevant to the person, topic, quotation, historical context, research population, or learning objective.
source_summary.Possible Recommendation: Replace unnecessary gender-specific wording with inclusive alternatives and avoid unnecessary assumptions about gender.
source_summary.Research Basis: Generic pronouns, occupational bias, exclusionary bias, and structural/contextual bias are identified in textual gender-bias research (Kanij et al., 2025).

criteria.Definition: Use of gender-specific pronouns for a generic or unspecified person where gender is irrelevant.
criteria.Indicators: Generic he/him/his or she/her; pronoun assigned to an unspecified occupation or participant.
criteria.Potential Concern Examples: Every programmer should submit his code.; A nurse should ensure she updates the record.
criteria.Non-Concern Examples: John should submit his code.; Every programmer should submit their code.
criteria.Context Considerations: A gendered pronoun is not automatically problematic when referring to a known individual. Consider whether the person’s gender is known and relevant.
criteria.Possible Recommendation: Replace unnecessary gender-specific pronouns with neutral alternatives such as they/their.
criteria.Research Basis: Generic pronouns are identified as a form of textual gender bias in gender-bias taxonomies discussed by Kanij et al. (2025).

criteria.Definition: Use of unnecessarily gender-marked terminology for occupations or professional roles.
criteria.Indicators: Chairman, policeman, salesman, businessman, fireman; gender-marked role titles where gender is irrelevant.
criteria.Potential Concern Examples: Ask the chairman for approval.
criteria.Non-Concern Examples: Ask the chairperson for approval.; The historical document used the title chairman.
criteria.Context Considerations: Historical quotations or official role titles may legitimately contain gender-marked terminology.
criteria.Possible Recommendation: Use gender-neutral occupational terms where appropriate, e.g. chairperson, police officer, salesperson.
criteria.Research Basis: Occupational bias and explicit gender association with occupations/roles are identified in textual gender-bias research discussed by Kanij et al. (2025).

criteria.Definition: Gender-specific language used to address or collectively describe a mixed or unspecified group.
criteria.Indicators: Expressions such as hey guys or you guys when addressing an unspecified/mixed group.
criteria.Potential Concern Examples: Hey guys, please submit your assignments.
criteria.Non-Concern Examples: Hello everyone, please submit your assignments.
criteria.Context Considerations: Consider whether the term actually refers to a specific gendered group or is being quoted/discussed rather than used as an address.
criteria.Possible Recommendation: Use inclusive collective terms such as everyone, students, team, or class.
criteria.Research Basis: Broader exclusionary and structural gender-bias taxonomies support examining gendered wording used in otherwise gender-neutral contexts (Kanij et al., 2025).

criteria.CARE Category: Gendered Language – Gendered/Exclusionary Examples or Names
criteria.Definition: Unequal or stereotypical use of gender-associated characters or names within teaching examples.
criteria.Indicators: One gender repeatedly used for technical/positive examples; another associated with negative or less technical examples.
criteria.Potential Concern Examples: Male-named characters repeatedly succeed in programming examples while female-named characters repeatedly fail.
criteria.Non-Concern Examples: A teaching module uses varied characters without systematically associating their gender with success or failure.
criteria.Context Considerations: Do not infer gender from a name alone. Evaluate explicit gender information and broader patterns across several examples.
criteria.Possible Recommendation: Use varied characters and avoid systematically associating gender with positive, negative or technical outcomes.
criteria.Research Basis: CS instructional materials have been reported to assign negative roles disproportionately to characters with female names (Medel & Pournaghshband, as discussed in O'Brien et al., 2025).

criteria.Definition: Wording that unnecessarily assumes gender exists only within a male/female binary.
criteria.Indicators: Unnecessary male/female-only wording; exclusion of other gender identities where broader terminology would be appropriate.
criteria.Potential Concern Examples: Select your gender: Male / Female, when a binary classification is unnecessary to the activity.
criteria.Non-Concern Examples: This study compares outcomes reported for male and female participants, when those are the defined study populations.
criteria.Context Considerations: Binary categories may be appropriate when accurately reporting a dataset, study population or source. Consider the purpose before flagging.
criteria.Possible Recommendation: Where appropriate, use inclusive gender terminology or provide additional/self-described options.
criteria.Research Basis: GenderMag discusses gender identity/expression beyond a simple binary and cautions against designs that unnecessarily assume only male/female users.

source_summary.Definition: Content that reinforces stereotypical characteristics, behaviours, abilities, interests, learning approaches, or expectations based on gender.
source_summary.Scenarios / Indicators: Ability/competence; learning style; risk-taking; motivation/interest; personality/behaviour; hostile sexism; benevolent/patronising sexism.
source_summary.Potential Concern Examples: “Men are naturally better at programming.”; “Women are too cautious to experiment with unfamiliar software.”; “She is surprisingly good at programming for a woman.”
source_summary.Non-Concern Examples: “Students may use different approaches when learning new software.”; “The lecture examines stereotypes about women in computing.”
source_summary.Context Considerations: Discussion of a stereotype does not necessarily endorse it. Consider whether the content is explaining, quoting, criticising, or challenging the stereotype. Gender-correlated tendencies should not be treated as fixed characteristics of individuals.
source_summary.Possible Recommendation: Avoid unsupported gender generalisations and describe individual characteristics, behaviours, or evidence instead.
source_summary.Research Basis: Research identifies gender stereotypes relating to competence and sexism; GenderMag additionally considers learning style, self-efficacy, risk and motivation (Kanij et al., 2025; O'Brien et al., 2025).

criteria.Definition: Generalisation that one gender is naturally more or less capable in a subject, skill or technical activity.
criteria.Indicators: Claims about programming, mathematics, technical or problem-solving ability based on gender.
criteria.Potential Concern Examples: Men are naturally better at programming.
criteria.Non-Concern Examples: The study investigates whether gender differences exist in students’ computing experiences.
criteria.Context Considerations: Researching or criticising an ability stereotype does not mean the material endorses it.
criteria.Possible Recommendation: Remove gender-based generalisations and describe individual ability or research evidence instead.
criteria.Research Basis: Research describes negative assumptions about women's competence in CS/STEM contexts (O'Brien et al., 2025).

criteria.Definition: Assumption that a person's preferred way of learning technology can be determined solely by gender.
criteria.Indicators: Gender-based assumptions about following processes, instructions, exploration or tinkering.
criteria.Potential Concern Examples: Female students need step-by-step instructions, while male students prefer experimenting.
criteria.Non-Concern Examples: Different students may prefer structured instructions or experimentation.
criteria.Context Considerations: GenderMag identifies gender-correlated learning-style differences; these should not be interpreted as fixed characteristics of every person of a gender.
criteria.Possible Recommendation: Describe different learning approaches without assigning them automatically to genders.
criteria.Research Basis: GenderMag, as applied by O'Brien et al. (2025), uses learning style as a gender-correlated problem-solving facet rather than a universal gender characteristic.

criteria.Definition: Generalisation that willingness to take risks or experiment with technology is determined by gender.
criteria.Indicators: Claims that women are inherently cautious; men inherently take technological risks.
criteria.Potential Concern Examples: Women are too cautious to experiment with unfamiliar software.
criteria.Non-Concern Examples: Some students may be reluctant to experiment when an action could cause data loss.
criteria.Context Considerations: Risk attitude varies among individuals. GenderMag's facet represents a research-observed tendency, not a rule for individuals.
criteria.Possible Recommendation: Avoid assigning risk behaviour according to gender; describe the actual behaviour or situation instead.
criteria.Research Basis: Attitude toward risk is one of the problem-solving facets incorporated into GenderMag and used in the gender-bias assessment approach of O'Brien et al. (2025).

criteria.Definition: Assumption that interest in or motivation for using technology is inherently determined by gender.
criteria.Indicators: Claims about liking technology, programming or particular activities based on gender.
criteria.Potential Concern Examples: Boys enjoy programming because they naturally like technology more than girls.
criteria.Non-Concern Examples: Students have different motivations for learning programming.
criteria.Context Considerations: Do not convert population-level observations about motivation into assumptions about individuals.
criteria.Possible Recommendation: Describe the specific motivation or interest without attributing it inherently to gender.
criteria.Research Basis: Motivation is another GenderMag facet used to capture gender-correlated differences in approaches to technology (O'Brien et al., 2025).

criteria.Definition: Content assigning stereotypical personality traits or behaviours according to gender.
criteria.Indicators: Women described as emotional/passive; men as rational/assertive; gender-linked behavioural expectations.
criteria.Potential Concern Examples: Women are emotional while men are logical problem-solvers.
criteria.Non-Concern Examples: The case study examines stereotypes about gender and leadership behaviour.
criteria.Context Considerations: Determine whether the material endorses, reports, critiques or challenges the stereotype.
criteria.Possible Recommendation: Describe individuals based on their behaviour rather than gender-based assumptions.
criteria.Research Basis: Gender stereotypes and behavioural expectations are discussed as contextual forms of gender bias in the literature reviewed by Kanij et al. (2025).

criteria.Definition: Explicitly negative, demeaning or discriminatory statements about a gender.
criteria.Indicators: Claims of incompetence, inferiority or unsuitability based on gender.
criteria.Potential Concern Examples: Women are incompetent at work.
criteria.Non-Concern Examples: The lecturer explains why the statement ‘women are incompetent at work’ is sexist.
criteria.Context Considerations: Quoting a sexist statement to analyse or challenge it should not automatically be treated as endorsement.
criteria.Possible Recommendation: Remove discriminatory generalisations and use evidence-based, individual-focused language.
criteria.Research Basis: Hostile sexism is explicitly included in the textual gender-bias taxonomy discussed by Kanij et al. (2025).

criteria.Definition: Apparently positive or complimentary wording that still reinforces a gender stereotype or implies lowered expectations.
criteria.Indicators: Surprise at competence because of gender; paternalistic/patronising gender statements.
criteria.Potential Concern Examples: She is surprisingly good at programming for a woman.
criteria.Non-Concern Examples: She demonstrated strong programming skills in the assessment.
criteria.Context Considerations: Positive wording can still contain an underlying stereotypical assumption. Contextual interpretation is important.
criteria.Possible Recommendation: Remove the unnecessary gender comparison and describe the person's achievement directly.
criteria.Research Basis: Benevolent sexism is explicitly identified alongside hostile sexism in the taxonomy discussed by Kanij et al. (2025).

source_summary.Definition: Imbalance, limited representation, or systematically different portrayal of genders across examples, scenarios, characters, experts, or teaching content.
source_summary.Scenarios / Indicators: Numerical underrepresentation; expert/authority representation; participation/visibility imbalance; positive/negative character portrayal.
source_summary.Potential Concern Examples: Across 12 programming examples, 11 experts are men and one is a woman.; Male characters repeatedly appear as successful technical experts while female characters are repeatedly assigned negative roles.
source_summary.Non-Concern Examples: A single example involving a male programmer.; Teaching examples include people of different genders across technical and leadership roles.
source_summary.Context Considerations: Assess representation across multiple examples, sections, or the document rather than an isolated person. Do not infer gender from names alone.
source_summary.Possible Recommendation: Use a more balanced and diverse range of people, experts, characters, and examples where appropriate.
source_summary.Research Basis: Research reports gender underrepresentation and differences in the roles and representations given to characters in CS/SE educational material (O'Brien et al., 2025).

criteria.Definition: Persistent numerical imbalance in the genders represented across teaching examples or content.
criteria.Indicators: Repeated dominance of one gender; systematic absence/underrepresentation.
criteria.Potential Concern Examples: Across 12 programming examples, 11 experts are men and 1 is a woman.
criteria.Non-Concern Examples: One isolated example features a male programmer.
criteria.Context Considerations: Assess patterns across multiple examples rather than a single instance.
criteria.Possible Recommendation: Where appropriate, include a more balanced range of people in examples.
criteria.Research Basis: Persistent gender imbalance and underrepresentation in CS/SE education are reported in research reviewed by O'Brien et al. (2025).

criteria.Definition: One gender is repeatedly represented as the expert, authority or source of technical knowledge.
criteria.Indicators: Lecturers, researchers, experts or authority figures consistently represented by one gender.
criteria.Potential Concern Examples: All cybersecurity experts presented across a module are men.
criteria.Non-Concern Examples: One case study contains a male cybersecurity expert.
criteria.Context Considerations: Consider the overall pattern and whether representation accurately reflects a specific historical/source context.
criteria.Possible Recommendation: Include varied genders in expert and authority examples where appropriate.
criteria.Research Basis: Research into gender bias in CS/SE education identifies representation and male-dominated environments as relevant inclusivity concerns (O'Brien et al., 2025).

criteria.Definition: One gender is repeatedly portrayed as the active participant while others are absent or passive.
criteria.Indicators: Repeated active vs passive participation patterns; unequal visibility in technical activities.
criteria.Potential Concern Examples: Male students repeatedly perform programming tasks while women mainly observe.
criteria.Non-Concern Examples: Students of different genders participate in a range of technical activities.
criteria.Context Considerations: A single participant does not establish a pattern. Examine the wider section/document.
criteria.Possible Recommendation: Diversify who is shown actively participating in technical and learning activities.
criteria.Research Basis: Research links masculine CS environments and representation with belonging and participation concerns (O'Brien et al., 2025).

criteria.Definition: Systematic association of particular genders with positive or negative character outcomes.
criteria.Indicators: One gender repeatedly successful/competent; another repeatedly unsuccessful, problematic or dependent.
criteria.Potential Concern Examples: Female-named characters repeatedly fail while male-named characters solve the technical problems.
criteria.Non-Concern Examples: Characters of different genders appear across varied positive and negative situations without a systematic pattern.
criteria.Context Considerations: Do not infer gender from names alone. Evaluate explicit gender information and patterns across multiple examples.
criteria.Possible Recommendation: Avoid systematically associating a particular gender with negative outcomes or incompetence.
criteria.Research Basis: Research on CS instructional materials reported disproportionate negative roles for characters with female names (Medel & Pournaghshband, as discussed in O'Brien et al., 2025).

source_summary.Definition: Potential gender imbalance, stereotyping, objectification, or gender-coded representation within images and other visual teaching material.
source_summary.Scenarios / Indicators: Stereotypical imagery; gendered visual authority; gendered aesthetics/“pink it and shrink it”; technical-confidence portrayal; sexualised/objectifying imagery; masculine-coded imagery/environment.
source_summary.Potential Concern Examples: Images repeatedly show men programming while women assist.; Pink is consistently used for women and blue for men.; Unnecessary sexualised imagery of women is used in an image-processing example.
source_summary.Non-Concern Examples: An image contains a man working on a computer.; A diagram uses gender-neutral icons.; Different genders participate in technical activities.
source_summary.Context Considerations: Do not infer gender solely from appearance when unclear. Consider the image's purpose, captions, surrounding text, and overall visual pattern. A single image may not establish imbalance.
source_summary.Possible Recommendation: Use diverse and inclusive visual representations and avoid unnecessary stereotypical, gender-coded, or objectifying imagery.
source_summary.Research Basis: Research identifies gendered imagery, representation, sexualised imagery, and masculine-coded CS environments as relevant concerns (O'Brien et al., 2025; GenderMag).

criteria.Definition: Images repeatedly portray genders through stereotypical activities, characteristics or roles.
criteria.Indicators: Men shown programming; women assisting; stereotypical gender activities.
criteria.Potential Concern Examples: Several illustrations consistently show men programming while women take notes.
criteria.Non-Concern Examples: One image contains a man using a computer.
criteria.Context Considerations: Consider the overall visual pattern, image purpose, captions and surrounding text.
criteria.Possible Recommendation: Use varied and inclusive visual representations.
criteria.Research Basis: Research identifies differences in representation and imagery in CS educational material as potential sources of gender bias (O'Brien et al., 2025).

criteria.Definition: One gender is repeatedly visually portrayed as more authoritative, knowledgeable or powerful.
criteria.Indicators: Men repeatedly lead/present; women observe, assist or take notes.
criteria.Potential Concern Examples: Across multiple diagrams, men lead technical discussions while women assist.
criteria.Non-Concern Examples: An individual man presents one project while other materials show diverse leadership.
criteria.Context Considerations: Assess repeated patterns rather than isolated images.
criteria.Possible Recommendation: Represent different genders across leadership, expert and supporting positions.
criteria.Research Basis: Research on gendered representations and masculine CS environments supports examining how visual material communicates belonging and authority (O'Brien et al., 2025).

criteria.CARE Category: Visual Representation – Gendered Aesthetics / “Pink It and Shrink It”
criteria.Definition: Visual design unnecessarily relies on stereotypical gender colours or aesthetics.
criteria.Indicators: Pink consistently used for women; blue for men; stereotypically feminised/masculinised visual design.
criteria.Potential Concern Examples: A teaching graphic uses pink for all women and blue for all men.
criteria.Non-Concern Examples: Pink appears as part of a general colour palette with no gender association.
criteria.Context Considerations: Pink or blue is not inherently biased. Consider whether the colour is deliberately/repeatedly used to encode gender stereotypes.
criteria.Possible Recommendation: Avoid unnecessary stereotypical colour coding and use functionally meaningful or neutral visual design.
criteria.Research Basis: GenderMag literature discusses genderised aesthetics and stereotypical design approaches such as “pink it and shrink it.”

criteria.Definition: Images repeatedly associate confidence or independence with technology with one gender.
criteria.Indicators: Men confidently operating systems; women appearing confused, hesitant or dependent on assistance.
criteria.Potential Concern Examples: Male students are repeatedly shown confidently coding while female students require help.
criteria.Non-Concern Examples: People of different genders are shown with varied levels of experience and confidence.
criteria.Context Considerations: Confidence cannot reliably be inferred from gender or appearance alone. Consider captions, actions and repeated patterns.
criteria.Possible Recommendation: Avoid repeatedly associating technological confidence or dependency with gender.
criteria.Research Basis: This scenario relates to the computer self-efficacy facet used by GenderMag and the literature linking masculine CS environments with women's confidence (O'Brien et al., 2025).

criteria.Definition: Unnecessary sexualisation or objectification of a gender in educational visual material.
criteria.Indicators: Sexualised stock images; objectifying portrayals unrelated to learning purpose.
criteria.Potential Concern Examples: A programming/image-processing exercise unnecessarily uses a sexualised image of a woman.
criteria.Non-Concern Examples: A medical lesson uses relevant anatomical imagery for a legitimate educational purpose.
criteria.Context Considerations: Consider educational relevance and purpose. The presence of a body/person is not automatically objectification.
criteria.Possible Recommendation: Replace unnecessary sexualised/objectifying imagery with learning-relevant alternatives.
criteria.Research Basis: Research reports the historical use of a Playboy centrefold image in image-processing teaching materials as an example of gender bias (Medel & Pournaghshband, as discussed in O'Brien et al., 2025).

criteria.Definition: Visual material repeatedly uses imagery or design associated with stereotypically masculine computing culture.
criteria.Indicators: Masculine-coded pictures, objects, symbols or webpage design that repeatedly signals who belongs in computing.
criteria.Potential Concern Examples: A CS course webpage is dominated by stereotypically masculine imagery.
criteria.Non-Concern Examples: A technical image appears because it is directly relevant to the subject.
criteria.Context Considerations: Individual visual elements should not automatically be labelled masculine/feminine. Consider combinations, repetition and research-supported context.
criteria.Possible Recommendation: Use inclusive and varied visual environments that avoid unnecessarily signalling that computing belongs to one gender.
criteria.Research Basis: Masculine-stereotyped CS webpages were associated with lower confidence, belonging and enrolment intention among women in research discussed by O'Brien et al. (2025).

source_summary.Definition: Repeated or stereotypical association of genders with occupations, technical positions, leadership roles, support roles, or responsibilities.
source_summary.Scenarios / Indicators: Gendered division of labour; leadership vs support roles; technical vs non-technical roles; gender-assigned occupational expectations.
source_summary.Potential Concern Examples: “Professors are men and elementary teachers are women.”; Men repeatedly appear as engineers/team leaders while women are shown in administrative or support roles.
source_summary.Non-Concern Examples: “The software engineer developed the application while the project manager coordinated the project.”; A woman is a project manager and a man is a developer in one factual example.
source_summary.Context Considerations: An individual legitimately holding a particular role is not itself a concern. Consider repeated patterns and whether the material reinforces, reports, or challenges occupational stereotypes.
source_summary.Possible Recommendation: Use varied and inclusive examples of genders across technical, leadership, professional, and supporting roles.
source_summary.Research Basis: Occupational bias, gendered division of labour, and gendered roles/duties are identified in textual gender-bias research (Kanij et al., 2025).

criteria.CARE Category: Professional Roles – Gendered Division of Labour
criteria.Definition: Different occupations or types of work are stereotypically assigned according to gender.
criteria.Indicators: Men associated with technical/professional work; women with caring/support work.
criteria.Potential Concern Examples: Professors are men and elementary teachers are women.
criteria.Non-Concern Examples: The professor presented the lecture and the teacher facilitated the workshop.
criteria.Context Considerations: Factual descriptions of real individuals are not automatically concerns. Look for generalisation or repeated patterns.
criteria.Possible Recommendation: Use varied genders across occupations and avoid presenting occupational divisions as natural gender differences.
criteria.Research Basis: Gendered Division of Labor is explicitly identified as occupational bias in the taxonomy discussed by Kanij et al. (2025).

criteria.CARE Category: Professional Roles – Leadership vs Support Roles
criteria.Definition: Gender is repeatedly associated with different levels of authority or responsibility.
criteria.Indicators: Men as managers/leaders; women as assistants/note-takers/support staff.
criteria.Potential Concern Examples: Men repeatedly lead software teams while women organise meetings and take notes.
criteria.Non-Concern Examples: A woman is a project manager and a man is a developer in one factual scenario.
criteria.Context Considerations: Examine repeated patterns. An individual holding a particular position is not evidence of bias by itself.
criteria.Possible Recommendation: Diversify leadership and supporting roles across genders.
criteria.Research Basis: Gender-bias research identifies gendered roles and duties as occupational bias (Kanij et al., 2025).

criteria.CARE Category: Professional Roles – Technical vs Non-Technical Roles
criteria.Definition: Technical expertise is repeatedly associated with one gender while another is associated with non-technical work.
criteria.Indicators: Men as developers/engineers; women as HR/administration/support.
criteria.Potential Concern Examples: Male characters are software developers while female characters are administrative assistants across the examples.
criteria.Non-Concern Examples: Different genders are represented across technical and non-technical roles.
criteria.Context Considerations: Consider the pattern across the material rather than individual legitimate occupations.
criteria.Possible Recommendation: Include varied genders in technical and non-technical professional roles.
criteria.Research Basis: Occupational bias and gendered assignment of roles/duties are recognised forms of textual gender bias (Kanij et al., 2025).

criteria.Definition: Content explicitly suggests that particular careers or responsibilities naturally suit a particular gender.
criteria.Indicators: Claims that men/women are naturally suited to specific occupations.
criteria.Potential Concern Examples: Men make good computer scientists while women are better suited to nursing.
criteria.Non-Concern Examples: This study examines women's representation in nursing and computing professions.
criteria.Context Considerations: Discussion of an occupational stereotype is different from endorsing it. Consider historical/research context.
criteria.Possible Recommendation: Remove gender-based occupational assumptions and focus on skills, qualifications and individual interests.
criteria.Research Basis: GenderMag materials discuss stereotypical societal expectations connecting gender with occupations, while occupational bias is also identified in textual gender-bias taxonomies (Kanij et al., 2025).
